idiom_name: bidirectional membrane wrapper + per-membrane identity map + whole-membrane revoker
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: interpose one wrapper between the two sides of a subsystem boundary and make it the only route across. On every invocation the wrapper wraps each capability argument before forwarding it inward, and wraps whatever comes back - returned objects, callbacks, iterators, error payloads - before handing it outward; the same rule applies to calls originating on the protected side, so neither side ever holds a raw reference to the other. Keep a per-membrane identity map from wrapped object to wrapper so a given object always yields the same wrapper (identity, equality and caching stay stable, and repeated crossings do not multiply wrappers), and hold its entries weakly so the map does not keep the graph alive. Revocation belongs to the membrane, not to individual references: one flag or generation counter, checked and used atomically before forwarding, invalidates every reference ever handed out through it. The wrapped objects never change - the policy lives in the wrapper - which is what lets the subsystem stay unaware that it is mediated. The structure is hand-written in every language; what varies is how the host supplies the interception hook and the weak identity map.
code_sketch:
membrane.wrap(ref) -> wrapper          # identity map: same object -> same wrapper
on call(wrapper, args):
    if revoked: raise                  # check and forward atomically
    inner_args = [membrane.wrap(a) for a in args]    # wrap the way in
    result = forward(wrapper.target, inner_args)
    return membrane.wrap(result)       # wrap the way out (objects, callbacks, iterators)
revoke(membrane)                       # kills every wrapper the membrane emitted
pitfalls: Wrapping only one direction: an argument or a result that crosses raw gives the other side an unguarded route into the object graph, which is exactly the failure the pattern exists to prevent.
No identity map: the same object yields a new wrapper on every crossing, so equality and caching break and wrapper creation leaks memory.

Check-then-forward as two separate steps: under concurrency the revocation state can change between the check and the forward (the TOCTTOU flaw in the cited analysis); make the decision and the forward one atomic step.

Wrong move: mediate method calls but forward raw receivers, prototypes, descriptors or iterator internals -> a guest can recover authority through a later protocol step or reflection -> instead wrap every reachable operation and metadata path, not just ordinary calls.

Wrong move: treat a proxy as transparent identity across realms -> ===, Map/Set keys and type checks diverge and policy decisions become inconsistent -> instead maintain one per-membrane identity map and define explicit equality and type behavior.

Wrong move: use an in-process membrane as the only defense against hostile native or reflective code -> raw references, FFI or host escapes bypass interception -> instead use an unforgeable-reference runtime and layer process or VM isolation for hostile code.
